polity-1.title: Constitutional foundations: authority with limits

sections.heading: Why a constitution matters
sections.text: A constitution establishes institutions, distributes power and expresses commitments about political life. Constitutionalism adds the idea that power should be limited and accountable. A written document alone cannot guarantee that idea in practice. Ask how rules, courts, representation and public conduct make authority answerable, and how citizens can seek a remedy when a commitment is violated.

sections.heading: Connect rights and social conditions
sections.text: Formal equality means little if people cannot access institutions or challenge discrimination. Distinguish equal legal status from measures intended to address disadvantage. Fundamental rights, directive principles and duties have different constitutional roles; they should not be treated as one interchangeable list. Use the official constitutional text to check wording and provisions rather than relying on a remembered slogan.

sections.heading: Explain democracy beyond an election
sections.text: Elections enable selection and removal of representatives, but democracy also needs public reasoning, accountability, liberties and participation between elections. Diversity does not automatically lead to conflict: institutions can accommodate differences through representation and power-sharing. A good answer explains how a mechanism works and recognises its limitations instead of merely calling an institution democratic.

practice.question: How can equal treatment and support for disadvantaged groups be compatible?
practice.answer: Identical treatment can preserve unequal starting conditions. Carefully designed measures can improve substantive access while remaining subject to constitutional justification, limits and review.

polity-2.title: Institutions: separate functions, shared accountability

sections.heading: Follow the decision through institutions
sections.text: Instead of memorising an office in isolation, trace how a public decision is proposed, authorised, implemented and reviewed. Legislatures deliberate and authorise; executives administer; courts decide legal disputes and review according to their jurisdiction. Their functions overlap in defined ways. The presence of overlap does not mean there are no limits or that each institution can assume every role.

sections.heading: Distinguish responsibility and independence
sections.text: Political executives in a parliamentary system are answerable through legislative mechanisms, while permanent administration operates under a different set of responsibilities. Judicial independence protects adjudication from improper pressure, but is not a claim that judicial institutions are beyond all accountability. Explain the particular mechanism—questions, committees, financial scrutiny or reasoned judgments—rather than simply praising checks and balances.

sections.heading: Read federal relations in context
sections.text: Federalism distributes authority across levels of government. Legislative competence, administrative cooperation and fiscal resources are distinct dimensions. A function assigned on paper may be difficult to perform without staff or funds. Conflicts should be analysed through institutional arrangements and constitutional procedures. Verify current provisions and judgments before adding contemporary legal claims to an exam answer.

practice.question: Why can a legislative committee add value beyond a floor debate?
practice.answer: Committees can examine detailed evidence, question officials and scrutinise specific subjects with continuity. Their value depends on information, deliberation, follow-up and the powers available to them.

mcq: Which approach best examines an institution?
Institutions are understood through what they can do, how they act and how their actions are scrutinised.

polity-3.title: Governance: turn a right into a working service

sections.heading: The implementation chain
sections.text: A policy announcement is not the same as service delivery. Trace eligibility, application, verification, decision, payment or provision, and grievance resolution. Each step may exclude people through distance, documentation, language or discretion. Distinguish the legal promise, administrative design and actual outcome. An effective answer specifies where the failure occurs before proposing a reform.

sections.heading: Local government and participation
sections.text: Decentralisation can improve responsiveness when functions, funds and staff support one another. Merely creating an elected local body does not ensure meaningful authority. Participation should include people who have less time, literacy or social influence. Public meetings, disclosure and social audit can help, but their effectiveness depends on access to information and a response to the issues raised.

sections.heading: Technology is one part of the system
sections.text: Digitisation may reduce repeated paperwork and improve tracking, but can also create exclusion when authentication fails or connectivity is poor. Build an assisted or offline route and an appeal mechanism into the design. Accountability requires responsibility and correction, not only a dashboard. Use a citizen’s experience to connect institutional rules with measurable outcomes.

practice.answer: An authorised assisted or alternative verification route, a recorded complaint, time-bound review and protection against arbitrary denial. The objective is both integrity of delivery and meaningful access.
